# How to use this subject

Applied Sociology is a theory course of the first semester (3 credits, 60 hours). It is mostly definitions, characteristics, types, differences and the role of the nurse, so it rewards neat, well-structured answers. Study one notes file a day: read it once, close it, write the definitions and the "difference between" tables from memory, then answer the question bank for that unit.

## How the notes follow the INC syllabus

The INC course has seven units. Some are tiny and some are very large, so they have been arranged into eight notes files:

| Notes file | INC unit(s) | Hours |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 Introduction, basic concepts and social groups | Unit I (Introduction) joined with the first part of Unit II (society, community, association, institution, individual and society, personal disorganization, social groups) | 1 + part of 15 |
| 2 Social processes, socialization, social change and communities | Rest of Unit II (social processes, socialization, social change, urban/rural/tribal communities, importance of social structure) | part of 15 |
| 3 Culture | Unit III | 8 |
| 4 Family and marriage | Unit IV | 8 |
| 5 Social stratification | Unit V | 8 |
| 6 Social organization, social control and disorganization | First part of Unit VI | part of 15 |
| 7 Social problems, vulnerable groups, rights and welfare | Second part of Unit VI | part of 15 |
| 8 Clinical sociology | Unit VII | 5 |

Units II and VI carry 15 hours each, so expect the most questions from notes files 1, 2, 6 and 7.

## Exam pattern

Applied Sociology is **Section A (37 marks)** of a combined 3-hour university paper of 75 marks. **Section B (38 marks) is Applied Psychology.** Use about half the paper time (around 90 minutes) for Sociology.

| Part of Section A | Marks |
| --- | --- |
| MCQ | 6 × 1 = 6 |
| Essay (long answer) | 1 × 10 = 10 |
| Short answer | 3 × 5 = 15 |
| Very short answer | 3 × 2 = 6 |
| **Total** | **37** |

The INC pattern (Appendix 3) has no internal choice: answer every question. Internal assessment (continuous assessment and sessional exams) is added to the university marks as your university directs. Confirm the exact pattern and any choice with your university.

The mock tests in this subject:

- **Section A: Applied Sociology (37 marks, 90 minutes)** – the Sociology section of the combined paper.
- **Quick MCQ test** – 20 questions in 20 minutes.

## Probability ratings

- **High** – asked again and again in most university papers; prepare a complete answer with definition, points, a table and the nursing role.
- **Medium** – asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** – less common; useful for MCQs and very short answers.

These ratings are estimates from syllabus weight and common question patterns, not a promise of what will be asked.

## Topics that keep coming back

| Notes file | Favourite topics |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Definition, nature and scope of sociology; significance of sociology in nursing; primary vs secondary groups; community vs association |
| 2 | Social processes (cooperation, competition, conflict, accommodation, assimilation); socialization and its agencies; social change and role of nurse; rural vs urban community; health problems of rural, urban and tribal people |
| 3 | Characteristics of culture; culture and civilization; impact of culture and modernization on health; transcultural nursing |
| 4 | Types and functions of family; forms of marriage; marriage legislation; effect of family on health |
| 5 | Characteristics of caste; caste vs class; social mobility; influence of caste and class on health |
| 6 | Social control (aims, agencies); social disorganization (causes, control); social system; voluntary agencies |
| 7 | Poverty, dowry, child labour, substance abuse, juvenile delinquency, HIV/AIDS; vulnerable groups; fundamental rights of women and children; role of nurse |
| 8 | Clinical sociology; crisis intervention; services for the abused |

## Scoring tips for this subject

1. **Begin every answer with a definition**, and name the sociologist where you can (Comte, Tylor, MacIver, Cooley, Ghurye, Sorokin, Caplan).
2. **Use tables for "difference between" questions** – primary vs secondary group, community vs association, culture vs civilization, caste vs class, rural vs urban, competition vs conflict, accommodation vs assimilation. Six to eight rows earn full marks.
3. **Write characteristics as numbered points with a heading word** ("1. Universality – …").
4. **Always end with "Role of the nurse"** or "Application in nursing" – examiners in a nursing paper look for this link, even when the question does not ask for it directly.
5. **Give Indian examples** – joint family, caste, Sanskritization, dowry, tribal communities, national schemes.
6. **For legislation questions**, write the name and year of the Act and two or three main points. Do not invent section numbers or figures.
7. **Draw a simple diagram** where it helps – classification of social processes, forms of marriage, agencies of socialization, phases of crisis.
8. **For the 10-mark essay**, plan a structure: introduction and definition → characteristics or types → causes or factors → effects on health → role of the nurse → conclusion.
9. Very short answers (2 marks): one-line definition plus two points or one example.
10. Keep Sociology to about 90 minutes so that Psychology (Section B) gets its fair share of time.

## One-line definitions

- **Sociology** – scientific study of society, social relationships, groups and institutions.
- **Society** – web of social relationships.
- **Community** – people in a definite locality with a common life and we-feeling.
- **Association** – group organised for a specific purpose.
- **Institution** – established procedure for meeting a social need (marriage).
- **Social group** – two or more people who interact and share a sense of unity.
- **Socialization** – lifelong learning of culture, norms and roles.
- **Social change** – change in social structure and relationships over time.
- **Culture** – learned, shared, transmitted way of life.
- **Family** – group united by marriage, blood or adoption, sharing a home.
- **Marriage** – socially approved union regulating sex and legitimising children.
- **Social stratification** – ranking of people in layers with unequal rewards.
- **Caste** – hereditary, endogamous group with fixed rank.
- **Class** – group with similar wealth, occupation and education; open.
- **Social mobility** – movement from one social position to another.
- **Social control** – means by which society makes members conform.
- **Social disorganization** – breakdown of harmony and relationships in society.
- **Social problem** – harmful condition affecting many, needing collective action.
- **Clinical sociology** – applied sociology that assesses and changes social situations.
- **Crisis** – acute upset when usual coping fails; time-limited.

## Must-know lists

- **Nature of sociology**: independent, social, categorical, pure, abstract, generalizing, rational and empirical.
- **Social processes**: associative – cooperation, accommodation, assimilation; dissociative – competition, conflict; plus isolation.
- **Agencies of socialization**: family (first), peers, school, religion, community, media, workplace, state.
- **Characteristics of culture**: learned, shared, transmitted, social, adaptive, dynamic, integrated, varies.
- **Leininger**: preservation, accommodation, repatterning.
- **Types of family**: nuclear, joint, extended; patrilineal, matrilineal; patrilocal, matrilocal, neolocal.
- **MacIver's essential functions of family**: sex need, reproduction and child rearing, home.
- **Forms of marriage**: monogamy, polygyny, polyandry (fraternal, non-fraternal), group marriage.
- **Ghurye's caste features**: segmental division, hierarchy, feeding restrictions, disabilities and privileges, hereditary occupation, endogamy.
- **Mobility**: horizontal, vertical (up, down), intergenerational, intragenerational.
- **Race criteria**: skin, hair, cephalic index, nasal index, stature, eyes, blood groups.
- **Social control**: formal (law, police, courts) and informal (family, religion, customs, public opinion).
- **Norms**: folkways (mild) → mores (strong) → laws (formal).
- **Sick role (Parsons)**: excused from duties; not blamed; must want to recover; must seek help.
- **Crisis types**: maturational, situational, adventitious.
- **Crisis steps**: assessment → planning → intervention → resolution → anticipatory planning.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: sociology is the scientific study of human society, social relationships, groups and institutions and how they change. The term was coined by Auguste Comte (father of sociology). MacIver and Page: sociology is about social relationships, the network of which is society.
2. Nature: an independent science; a social, not physical, science; categorical (describes what is, not what ought to be); a pure science whose findings are applied; abstract; generalizing; both rational and empirical.
3. Scope – formal (specialistic) school (Simmel, Weber, Tönnies): study only the forms of social relationships such as cooperation, competition and conflict.
4. Scope – synthetic school (Durkheim, Hobhouse, Sorokin): sociology is a general science of society as a whole, drawing on all social sciences.
5. Practical scope: social structure, processes, institutions, stratification, culture, socialization, social control, social change, social problems, medical, rural, urban and clinical sociology.
6. Significance in nursing: understanding the patient as a social being in a family and community; respecting culture, beliefs and customs; recognising social causes of disease (poverty, overcrowding, illiteracy, addiction).
7. Helps in community health nursing – knowing village structure, leaders and health practices; planning health education suited to the group.
8. Helps understand the hospital as a social system – roles, status, teamwork; identifies vulnerable groups; supports rehabilitation and adjustment to social change.
9. Conclusion: sociology enables holistic, culturally appropriate, family- and community-centred nursing care.
questions.question: Define sociology. Explain its nature and scope, and describe the significance of sociology in nursing.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: two or more people who interact, share a sense of unity (we-feeling) and have common interests or goals. An aggregate such as a bus-stop crowd is not a group.
2. Characteristics: two or more members; reciprocal interaction; sense of unity; common interest; group norms; structure of roles and leadership; dynamic nature.
3. Classification: primary and secondary (Cooley); in-group and out-group (Sumner); voluntary and involuntary; small and large; formal and informal; temporary and permanent; reference group (Hyman, Merton); Gemeinschaft and Gesellschaft (Tönnies).
4. Primary vs secondary: example – family, play group vs hospital, trade union; size – small vs large; contact – face to face, intimate vs indirect, formal; relationship – personal, for its own sake vs impersonal, for a purpose; duration – long lasting vs may be temporary; control – informal (praise, blame) vs formal (rules, law); role – shapes personality ('nursery of human nature') vs meets special needs.
5. Importance in nursing: the family is the first caregiver and decision maker; patients form ward groups; group health teaching and support groups (diabetes, cancer, de-addiction); the nursing team is a formal group needing clear roles; reference groups shape health behaviour such as smoking among adolescents.
questions.question: What is a social group? Explain its characteristics and classification, and differentiate between primary and secondary groups. Add a note on the importance of groups in nursing.

questions.answer:
1. Meaning: community – people in a definite locality sharing a common life and we-feeling; association – people deliberately organised for a specific purpose.
2. Origin: community grows naturally; association is deliberately formed.
3. Membership: by birth or residence vs voluntary.
4. Duration: permanent vs may end when its aim is met.
5. Scope: community meets most needs of life; association meets a limited purpose.
6. Rules: community governed by customs; association by a written constitution and office bearers.
7. Examples: a village vs Trained Nurses' Association of India.
questions.question: Differentiate between community and association.

questions.answer:
Society is a web of social relationships (MacIver and Page).
1. Likeness – shared needs, language and culture.
2. Difference – variety of age, sex and occupation, allowing division of labour.
3. Interdependence – no member is self-sufficient.
4. Cooperation and conflict – both exist; cooperation holds society together, controlled conflict brings change.
5. Abstract – relationships cannot be seen.
6. Dynamic – it keeps changing.
7. Has a culture of its own.
8. Wider than any group – includes many groups, communities and institutions.
questions.question: Explain the characteristics of society.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: a state in which an individual's behaviour deviates from accepted norms so that he cannot fulfil social roles and personal life breaks down (Elliott and Merrill).
2. Forms: alcoholism and drug addiction, crime, delinquency, suicide, prostitution, mental illness, beggary, gambling.
3. Causes: personal – illness, disability, frustration; family – broken home, violence, neglect; economic – poverty, unemployment, debt; social – rapid change, migration, bad company; cultural – conflict of old and new values.
4. Role of the nurse: identify early signs, listen without judging, refer to counsellor, de-addiction centre or social worker, involve the family, teach healthy coping.
questions.question: What is personal disorganization? Explain its causes and the role of the nurse.

questions.answer:
1. The relationship is two-way: society shapes the individual and the individual shapes society.
2. Social contract theory (Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau): people agreed to form society; criticised as unhistorical.
3. Organic theory (Spencer): society is like a body, individuals its cells; ignores free will.
4. Modern view: individual and society make each other through socialization and social action.
5. Evidence: children reared in isolation (Kamala and Amala, Anna) did not develop language or normal behaviour.
6. Society gives protection, culture, language, education, identity, status and role; the individual gives work, ideas, leadership and passes on culture.
questions.question: Discuss the relationship between the individual and society.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: repeated forms of social interaction between individuals or groups (Ginsberg).
2. Associative processes bring people together; dissociative processes push them apart.
3. Cooperation: working together for a common goal; direct (doing the same work) and indirect (division of labour); primary, secondary, tertiary. Example: doctor, nurse and family cooperating in a care plan.
4. Accommodation: conscious adjustment to conflict while differences remain; methods – coercion, compromise, arbitration, conciliation, toleration, conversion, sublimation, rationalization. Example: a new nurse adjusting to ward routine.
5. Assimilation: slow, unconscious merging of cultures so that differences fade; helped by tolerance, long contact, intermarriage; hindered by prejudice and isolation. Example: migrants adopting city ways.
6. Competition: impersonal, continuous, rule-bound struggle for limited things; raises efficiency but excess causes anxiety. Example: competition for nursing seats.
7. Conflict: personal, conscious, intermittent struggle to defeat a rival; types – personal, racial, class, political, international (Gillin and Gillin); can be harmful but may bring change. Example: quarrel between relatives and staff.
8. Isolation: absence of interaction – physical, social (stigma of leprosy, HIV, mental illness) or psychological (loneliness of elders).
9. Nursing relevance: promote cooperation and teamwork, resolve conflicts through accommodation, reduce isolation by communication and fighting stigma.
questions.question: What are social processes? Describe the associative and dissociative social processes with examples from nursing.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: the lifelong process by which a person learns the culture, norms, values and roles of society and becomes a functioning member.
2. Characteristics: lifelong; transmits culture; learned through interaction; varies between societies; builds self and personality; conscious or unconscious.
3. Process – Cooley's looking-glass self: imagining how we appear to others, how they judge us, and feeling pride or shame.
4. Mead: the self has 'I' and 'me'; stages – imitation, play stage (one role at a time), game stage (many roles; the generalized other).
5. Freud: superego formed by taking in parents' and society's rules.
6. Life stages: primary socialization (infancy), secondary (school, peers), adult, anticipatory (learning a role before taking it), resocialization (after retirement, disability, hospitalisation, migration).
7. Agencies: family – first and most important; peer group; school; religion; neighbourhood; mass media and internet; workplace; state and law.
8. Role of the nurse: professional socialization of students; helping patients learn the sick role and new routines (insulin, diet); teaching families healthy habits as an agent of socialization for health.
questions.question: Define socialization. Explain its characteristics, process and agencies. Add the role of the nurse.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: change in social structure and social relationships of a society over time (MacIver and Page).
2. Nature: universal; continuous with varying speed; community change; unpredictable in detail; planned or unplanned; value-neutral (progress or regress).
3. Factors: demographic (population growth, ageing, migration); technological (vaccines, mobile phones); economic (industrialization); cultural (ideas, education); political and legal (new laws); biological and natural (epidemics, floods); communication and media.
4. Process: invention, discovery, diffusion, acculturation; Indian processes – Sanskritization (Srinivas), Westernization, modernization, urbanization.
5. Cultural lag (Ogburn): material culture changes faster than beliefs.
6. Theories: linear, cyclical, conflict (Marx), functional (Parsons).
7. Role of the nurse: change agent, health educator, researcher, adapting to new technology, advocate, counsellor, leader who plans change step by step.
questions.question: Define social change. Discuss its nature, factors and the role of the nurse in social change.

questions.answer:
1. Size and density: small and scattered vs large and dense.
2. Occupation: agriculture vs industry, trade and services.
3. Relationships: primary and personal vs secondary and impersonal.
4. Family: joint more common vs nuclear more common.
5. Social control: informal (customs, elders, panchayat) vs formal (law, police).
6. Mobility: low vs high.
7. Social change: slow vs fast.
8. Services: fewer vs more but unequal; health problems – communicable disease vs lifestyle disease and pollution.
questions.question: Differentiate between rural and urban community.

questions.answer:
1. Rural: communicable diseases (diarrhoea, typhoid, TB), malnutrition and anaemia, maternal and child health problems, unsafe water and open defecation, snake bite and farm injuries, pesticide poisoning, distance from care, dependence on untrained practitioners.
2. Urban: diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, cancer, obesity, air and noise pollution, road accidents, stress and mental illness, substance abuse, slum problems (TB, vector-borne disease), HIV and STIs, occupational disease.
3. Tribal: malaria and vector-borne disease, malnutrition, anaemia, sickle cell disease in some groups, maternal and infant illness, skin and worm infections, alcohol use, poor access to services, mistrust of outsiders.
questions.question: Describe the major health problems of rural, urban and tribal communities.

questions.answer:
1. Competition is a struggle for limited things; conflict is a struggle to defeat or harm the rival.
2. Competition is impersonal; conflict is personal.
3. Competition is often unconscious of the rival; conflict is conscious.
4. Competition is continuous; conflict is intermittent.
5. Competition follows rules; conflict may involve threat or violence.
6. Competition usually promotes progress; conflict is mainly disruptive but may bring change.
7. Examples: competition for nursing seats vs quarrel between relatives and staff.
questions.question: Differentiate between competition and conflict.

questions.answer:
1. Accommodation is adjustment to conflict; assimilation is merging of cultures.
2. Accommodation is conscious; assimilation is unconscious.
3. Accommodation is quick; assimilation is slow.
4. In accommodation differences remain; in assimilation they disappear.
5. Accommodation may be temporary; assimilation is lasting.
6. Methods of accommodation: compromise, arbitration, toleration, conversion; aids to assimilation: tolerance, long contact, intermarriage.
7. Examples: a new nurse adjusting to ward routine vs migrants adopting city culture.
questions.question: Differentiate between accommodation and assimilation.

questions.answer: A term given by W. F. Ogburn for the gap that arises when material culture (technology) changes faster than non-material culture (beliefs and customs).
questions.question: What is cultural lag?

questions.answer: A process described by M. N. Srinivas in which a lower caste adopts the customs, rituals and way of life of a higher caste to raise its status.
questions.question: What is Sanskritization?

questions.answer: Family (the first and most important), peer group, school, religion; others include mass media, workplace and the state.
questions.question: Name four agencies of socialization.

questions.answer:
1. Definition (Tylor): culture is the complex whole of knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom and other capabilities and habits acquired as a member of society.
2. Components: material (houses, tools, medicines) and non-material (beliefs, values, norms, language).
3. Characteristics: learned, shared, transmitted, social, ideational, gratifies needs, adaptive, dynamic, integrated, varies between societies, superorganic.
4. Culture and health – positive: breastfeeding, hand washing before meals, family support, prayer giving comfort.
5. Harmful: discarding colostrum, food taboos in pregnancy, unhygienic cord care, belief in evil eye delaying care, going first to quacks, child marriage, tobacco and alcohol at social events, stigma of TB, leprosy, HIV and mental illness.
6. Modernization: adoption of science, technology, industry, urbanization, education and rational outlook.
7. Positive impact: control of infections by vaccines and sanitation, institutional delivery, longer life, health education, telemedicine, women's education.
8. Negative impact: lifestyle diseases (diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, cancer, obesity), stress and depression, substance abuse, accidents, pollution, loneliness of elderly in nuclear families, slums and TB.
9. Role of nurse: cultural assessment, respect beliefs, preserve helpful practices, negotiate and repattern harmful ones, promote healthy modern practices and warn of modern hazards.
questions.question: Define culture. Explain the characteristics of culture and discuss the impact of culture and modernization on health and disease.

questions.answer:
1. Transcultural society: people of many cultures living and working together, as in Indian cities and hospitals.
2. Transcultural nursing (Madeleine Leininger, Culture Care theory, Sunrise model): care that is sensitive to and congruent with the patient's culture.
3. Cultural diversity: different groups have different languages, religions, food, dress and customs; caused by geography, history, religion, migration, isolation.
4. Cultural uniformity: cultural universals – family, marriage rules, language, belief, care of the sick, rites at birth and death; in India 'unity in diversity'.
5. Related ideas: ethnocentrism, cultural relativism, culture shock, subculture.
6. Leininger's actions: culture care preservation (keep helpful practices), accommodation or negotiation (adjust care – diet, female staff), repatterning (gently change harmful practices).
7. Cultural competence: awareness of own biases, knowledge of cultures, culturally sensitive assessment, interpreters, respect for privacy, modesty and religious needs.
8. Conclusion: culturally competent care improves trust, compliance and outcomes.
questions.question: What is transcultural nursing? Explain cultural diversity and uniformity, and the nurse's role in a transcultural society.

questions.answer:
1. Meaning: culture is the way of life, values and ideas; civilization is material and technical achievement.
2. Nature: culture is internal, an end (what we are); civilization is external, a means (what we use) – MacIver.
3. Measurement: culture is hard to measure; civilization can be measured by efficiency.
4. Transmission: culture must be learned; civilization is easily borrowed.
5. Progress: culture does not always advance; civilization generally advances.
6. Examples: religion, art and values vs machines, hospitals and transport.
questions.question: Differentiate between culture and civilization.

questions.answer:
1. Material culture: objects made by people – houses, clothes, food, tools, vehicles, medicines, hospitals.
2. Non-material culture: ideas and behaviour.
3. Beliefs – ideas held to be true (evil eye causes illness).
4. Values – ideas of what is good (respect for elders).
5. Norms – folkways (mild, greeting), mores (strong, honesty), customs and laws (ban on dowry).
6. Language and symbols – means of sharing meaning (red cross).
7. Art, music and religion.
questions.question: Explain the components of culture.

questions.answer:
1. Socialization is the process by which culture is passed from one generation to the next.
2. Family, school, religion, peers and media teach language, values and norms.
3. Culture decides what is taught – obedience to elders in one culture, independence in another.
4. So culture is the content and socialization the channel.
5. Through socialization a child becomes a member of a culture; through culture, socialization gets its goals.
6. Health habits (diet, hygiene, health-seeking) are learned this way, so the nurse uses socialization agencies for health education.
questions.question: Explain the relationship between culture and socialization.

questions.answer:
1. Broad stages: hunting and gathering → domestication of animals → settled agriculture → villages and crafts → towns, trade and writing → industry and science → information society.
2. Invention – creating something new.
3. Discovery – finding something that existed.
4. Diffusion – spread of traits between societies (tea, cricket, modern medicine).
5. Acculturation – borrowing many traits through long contact.
6. Accumulation – new traits added to old ones.
7. Older labels such as savagery–barbarism–civilization are now rejected; cultural relativism treats each culture as meaningful in its own setting.
questions.question: Describe the evolution of culture and the ways in which culture grows.

questions.answer: Culture is that complex whole which includes knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom and any other capabilities and habits acquired by man as a member of society.
questions.question: Give Tylor's definition of culture.

questions.answer: Judging other cultures by the standards of one's own and regarding one's own culture as superior; in nursing it leads to disrespect and poor care.
questions.question: What is ethnocentrism?

questions.answer: Confusion and anxiety felt on entering an unfamiliar culture, for example a rural patient in a big city hospital or a nurse posted to a tribal area.
questions.question: What is culture shock?

questions.answer:
1. Definition: a group of persons united by marriage, blood or adoption, forming a household, interacting in social roles and sharing a common culture (Burgess and Locke).
2. Characteristics: universal; emotional basis; limited size; nuclear position in social structure; formative influence; responsibility of members; social regulation; permanent as an institution; common home; economic provision.
3. Types: by structure – nuclear, joint, extended; by marriage – monogamous, polygamous; by descent – patrilineal, matrilineal (Nair, Khasi, Garo); by residence – patrilocal, matrilocal, neolocal; by authority – patriarchal, matriarchal; family of orientation and procreation; newer forms – single-parent, blended.
4. Essential functions (MacIver): stable satisfaction of sex need, reproduction and child rearing, provision of a home.
5. Other functions: economic, educational, religious, recreational, protective, affectional, health, status giving.
6. Positive influence on health: source of health habits, home nursing, support in illness, birth spacing.
7. Negative influence: early marriage, consanguinity (inherited disorders), large families, domestic violence, son preference, broken homes, harmful taboos.
8. Role of nurse: involve family in care, family health education, identify and refer problems.
questions.question: Define family. Describe the characteristics, types and functions of the family. Add a note on the influence of family on health.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: a socially approved union of man and woman regulating sexual relations, legitimising children and creating rights and duties (Westermarck).
2. Forms: monogamy; polygamy – polygyny (one man, several wives) and polyandry (one woman, several husbands; fraternal as among the Todas, non-fraternal); group marriage.
3. Rules of mate selection: endogamy, exogamy, hypergamy (anuloma), hypogamy (pratiloma), cross-cousin marriage, levirate, sororate.
4. Hindu marriage traditionally a sacrament; Muslim nikah a civil contract with mahr.
5. Special Marriage Act 1954 – civil marriage irrespective of religion.
6. Hindu Marriage Act 1955 – monogamy, conditions, registration, void and voidable marriages, divorce including mutual consent.
7. Dowry Prohibition Act 1961 – giving, taking or demanding dowry is an offence.
8. Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 – protection orders, right to shared household.
9. Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006 – child is a boy under 21 or girl under 18; child marriage voidable; punishment.
10. Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act 2019 – instant triple talaq void and punishable.
11. Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 – dowry death (s. 80) and cruelty (ss. 85–86); Family Courts Act 1984 for conciliation.
questions.question: Define marriage. Describe the forms of marriage and the legislation related to marriage in India.

questions.answer:
Merits:
1. Security for the old, sick, widowed and disabled.
2. Shared work and resources.
3. Child care by grandparents.
4. Preserves culture and values.
5. Support in illness and crisis.
Demerits:
1. Lack of privacy and frequent quarrels.
2. Domination by the head; women and youth have little say.
3. Some members become idle and dependent.
4. Slows individual initiative.
5. Overcrowding may spread infection.
questions.question: Write the merits and demerits of the joint family.

questions.answer:
1. Family is the first source of habits – diet, hygiene, sleep, exercise.
2. Family support helps coping and home nursing; joint families help mothers and elderly.
3. Child marriage – early pregnancy, anaemia, obstructed labour, low birth weight, maternal and infant deaths.
4. Consanguineous marriage – inherited disorders such as thalassaemia.
5. Large families and poor spacing – malnutrition, maternal depletion.
6. Dowry and domestic violence – injury, depression, suicide.
7. Son preference – neglect of girls, sex selection.
8. Broken families – emotional problems, delinquency.
9. Multiple partners – STI and HIV risk.
10. Nurse: premarital and genetic counselling, family planning, identify violence and refer.
questions.question: Explain the influence of marriage and family on health and health practices.

questions.answer:
Customs: arranged marriages by elders, horoscope matching, engagement and wedding rituals (saptapadi, kanyadan, nikah), caste and gotra rules, dowry (illegal) and bride price among some tribes, child marriage (illegal), widow remarriage now accepted, rising inter-caste and love marriages.
Importance: regulates sex; gives legal status to children; forms the family and continues society; companionship and emotional security; economic cooperation; links families and builds kinship; passes on culture and property.
questions.question: Explain the social customs related to marriage in India and the importance of marriage.

questions.answer:
1. Joint families breaking into nuclear families.
2. Causes: industrialization, urbanization, migration for jobs, education, women's employment, new laws giving daughters property rights, individualism.
3. Changes in authority – more equality between husband and wife; children have more say.
4. Later marriage, fewer children, more inter-caste marriages, more divorces.
5. Functions shifted to outside agencies – schools, hospitals, crèches, insurance, old-age homes.
6. Effects: more freedom but less support for the elderly, child-care problems for working mothers, loneliness.
questions.question: Describe the changes taking place in the Indian family.

questions.answer: A child is a male who has not completed 21 years or a female who has not completed 18 years; marriage of a child is a child marriage.
questions.question: What is the legal age of marriage under the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006?

questions.answer: Endogamy is marriage within one's own group (caste, sub-caste, religion); exogamy is marriage outside a group such as one's gotra or clan.
questions.question: Differentiate between endogamy and exogamy.

questions.answer: A family in which descent and property pass through the mother, for example traditionally the Nairs of Kerala and the Khasi and Garo of Meghalaya.
questions.question: What is a matrilineal family? Give an example.

questions.answer:
1. Stratification: division of society into layers ranked by wealth, power, prestige or birth, with unequal rewards; universal, ancient, social, varied, consequential.
2. Caste: hereditary, endogamous group with traditional occupation and fixed rank, membership by birth; varna and jati.
3. Origin theories: traditional (Purusha Sukta), racial (Risley), political (Abbé Dubois), occupational (Nesfield), multiple-factor (Hutton).
4. Ghurye's features: segmental division; hierarchy; restrictions on feeding and social intercourse; civil and religious disabilities and privileges; lack of unrestricted choice of occupation; endogamy.
5. Positive: identity and security, caste council help, passing on skills, preserving culture, sense of order.
6. Negative: inequality and exploitation; untouchability (abolished by Article 17); blocks mobility and talent; casteism in politics; caste violence; opposes inter-caste marriage; barriers in health care.
7. Changes: Constitution and reservations, education, urbanization, industrialization, reform movements, Sanskritization and Westernization.
8. Health influence: occupational hazards, unequal access, purity–pollution beliefs, inherited disorders in small endogamous groups; nurse gives equal care and links families to schemes.
questions.question: Define social stratification. Describe the characteristics of the Indian caste system and its positive and negative impact on society.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: movement of a person or group from one social position to another (Sorokin).
2. Types: horizontal (same level, staff nurse moves hospital); vertical upward (staff nurse becomes superintendent) and downward; intergenerational (labourer's daughter becomes doctor); intragenerational (ward assistant becomes nurse); individual and group mobility.
3. Helping factors: education, new occupations, industrialization, urbanization, migration, democracy, reservations, marriage, ability.
4. Limiting factors: caste, poverty, poor health, illiteracy, gender discrimination, isolation.
5. Class and health: poor have more malnutrition, infections, TB, maternal and infant deaths, shorter life, delay in care; rich have more lifestyle disease but better access.
6. Caste and health: historical denial of water, school, care; occupational hazards (sanitation work); purity rules; inherited disorders.
7. Race and health: some inherited disorders more common (sickle cell in some tribal groups, thalassaemia in some communities); discrimination and language barriers; signs like cyanosis harder to see in dark skin.
8. Nurse: equal care, identify poor families, link to schemes, screening of high-risk groups.
questions.question: What is social mobility? Explain its types and factors. Discuss the influence of class, caste and race on health.

questions.answer:
1. Basis: birth vs wealth, occupation and education.
2. Nature: closed vs open.
3. Mobility: very little vs possible.
4. Marriage: endogamous vs no fixed rule.
5. Occupation: traditionally hereditary vs free choice.
6. Religious sanction: present vs absent.
7. Consciousness: strong caste feeling vs weaker class consciousness in India.
questions.question: Differentiate between caste and class.

questions.answer:
1. Slavery: one person owned by another; almost no mobility; ancient Greece and Rome.
2. Estate: based on land and law; rights fixed by law; feudal Europe – clergy, nobility, commoners.
3. Caste: based on birth; hereditary, closed; Indian caste system.
4. Class: based on wealth, income, occupation, education; open; upper, middle and lower classes.
5. All forms involve unequal wealth, power and prestige.
questions.question: Explain the forms of social stratification.

questions.answer:
1. Race: a large group sharing inherited physical features; now studied mainly as a social category, since human genetic variation is continuous.
2. Criteria: skin colour; hair form and colour; head form (cephalic index); nose form (nasal index); face and eye form (epicanthic fold); stature; blood groups and genetic markers.
3. Classifications: Caucasoid, Mongoloid, Negroid; for India Risley's seven types and B. S. Guha's six elements (Negrito, Proto-Australoid, Mongoloid, Mediterranean, Western Brachycephals, Nordic).
4. Racism – belief in superiority of one race; nursing ethics demand equal care.
questions.question: What is race? Explain the criteria of racial classification.

questions.answer:
1. Functionalist (Davis and Moore): important positions need rare skills; higher rewards attract able people.
2. Conflict (Marx): owners exploit workers; stratification causes conflict.
3. Weber: three dimensions – class, status, party.
4. Functions: motivation, placing people in key positions, order, identity.
5. Dysfunctions: inequality in income, education and health; exploitation; wasted talent; unrest.
questions.question: Explain the functions and theories of social stratification.

questions.answer: Ascribed status is given by birth (caste, sex, age); achieved status is earned by effort (registered nurse, doctor). The terms are from Ralph Linton.
questions.question: Differentiate ascribed and achieved status.

questions.answer: Change of position at the same social level, for example a staff nurse moving from one hospital to another as a staff nurse.
questions.question: What is horizontal mobility?

questions.answer: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form.
questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution abolished untouchability?

questions.answer:
1. Definition: the way society regulates the behaviour of members so they conform to norms and order is maintained; term popularised by E. A. Ross.
2. Aims: maintain order and stability; ensure conformity; protect society and the weak; bring unity; pass on culture; guide change.
3. Informal control: family, peer group, neighbourhood, religion, folkways, mores, customs, public opinion, praise, ridicule, gossip.
4. Formal control: law, police, courts, government, institutional rules, education system.
5. Positive control: rewards – praise, promotion, awards; negative control: punishment – blame, fines, suspension, jail.
6. Process: socialization (self-control), surveillance and feedback, sanctions, formal enforcement.
7. Norms, morals and values: folkways, mores, customs, laws, taboos; values are the basis of norms.
8. Role of the nurse: follow and teach rules and codes of ethics; health education as positive control; report legal violations; set an example.
questions.question: Define social control. Explain its aims, types and agencies, and the role of the nurse.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: a condition in which parts of the social system stop working in harmony and relationships break down (Elliott and Merrill); decrease in influence of social rules (Thomas and Znaniecki).
2. Symptoms: conflict of values, family breakdown, crime, delinquency, addiction, suicide, corruption, riots, unemployment, loss of trust, anomie (Durkheim).
3. Causes: rapid social change and cultural lag; industrialization and urbanization; value conflict; poverty and unemployment; disasters and epidemics; war; weak social control; population growth; individual factors.
4. Levels: personal, family and community disorganization.
5. Control and planning: strengthen the family (counselling, family courts); education; employment and social security; housing and urban planning; social legislation and enforcement; health services including mental health and de-addiction; recreation and youth programmes; voluntary agencies; coordinated welfare planning.
6. Role of the nurse: identify at-risk families, counselling and health education, referral, rehabilitation, participation in welfare programmes.
questions.question: What is social disorganization? Explain its symptoms, causes and measures for its control.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: a group people join by choice, usually non-profit, to serve a common interest or cause.
2. Characteristics: voluntary membership; definite aim; constitution and rules; democratic management; non-profit; often registered; funded by members, donations and grants.
3. Functions: fill gaps in government services, reach the poor, awareness, advocacy, disaster relief, training.
4. Examples: Indian Red Cross Society, Tuberculosis Association of India, Hind Kusht Nivaran Sangh, Family Planning Association of India, Indian Council for Child Welfare, HelpAge India, SEWA, Rotary and Lions clubs, self-help groups.
questions.question: What is a voluntary association? Write its characteristics and name some voluntary agencies working in health in India.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: a set of interacting individuals or groups organised around shared norms, roles and goals, forming a whole (Parsons).
2. Characteristics: interrelated parts; a goal; held together by norms and values; tends to equilibrium; boundaries but interacts with environment; dynamic.
3. Elements (Loomis): beliefs, sentiments, goals, norms, status-role, rank, power, sanctions, facilities.
4. Hospital: administrators, doctors, nurses, paramedical staff, patients and relatives interact; shared goal of recovery; rules and ethics; change in one part (staff shortage) affects others.
questions.question: Define social system. Explain its characteristics with the hospital as an example.

questions.answer:
1. Status: position held in a group (nurse, patient). Role: expected behaviour of that position; role is the dynamic aspect of status (Linton).
2. Role set: all roles linked to one status. Role conflict: incompatible demands of two roles; role strain: difficulty in one role.
3. The social system is a network of statuses and roles; when people perform roles, the system works.
4. Sick role (Parsons): (a) excused from normal duties, (b) not blamed for the illness, (c) expected to want to get well, (d) expected to seek competent help and cooperate.
questions.question: Explain role and status as structural elements of the social system. What is the sick role?

questions.answer:
1. Institutions depend on each other; change in one affects others.
2. Family and economy: earnings decide nutrition and health.
3. Family and education: parents' education shapes children's schooling.
4. Religion and family: rites of marriage, birth and death; food rules.
5. Economy and government: policies decide jobs, prices and welfare.
6. Health system depends on income, education, family, religion and policy.
7. Example chain: women's education → later marriage → smaller families → better child health.
questions.question: Explain the interrelationship of social institutions with examples.

questions.answer: Folkways are everyday customs whose breach brings only mild disapproval (table manners); mores are strong moral norms whose breach brings severe disapproval (honesty, respect for parents).
questions.question: Differentiate folkways and mores.

questions.answer: A state of normlessness in which social rules lose their hold on people, described by Émile Durkheim; a sign of social disorganization.
questions.question: What is anomie?

questions.answer: The orderly arrangement of individuals, groups, roles and institutions so that they work together in harmony to meet the needs of society.
questions.question: Define social organization.

questions.answer:
1. Social problem: a harmful condition affecting many people, with social causes, that needs collective action.
2. Poverty: inability to meet basic needs; absolute and relative.
3. Causes of poverty: unemployment, low farm productivity, large families, illiteracy, unequal assets, caste discrimination, illness, disasters, inflation.
4. Health effects: malnutrition, anaemia, low birth weight, infections, TB, poor maternal care, untreated disease.
5. Measures: MGNREGA, National Food Security Act, housing schemes, self-help groups, Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY, pensions under NSAP.
6. Substance abuse: harmful use of alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, opioids, inhalants leading to dependence.
7. Causes: peer pressure, curiosity, stress, family history, availability, advertising, unemployment.
8. Effects: liver disease, cancers, accidents, violence, HIV and hepatitis through needles, family breakdown, crime, job loss. Law: NDPS Act 1985.
9. Measures: de-addiction centres, counselling, Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, tobacco cessation, support groups.
10. Role of nurse: identify, health education, counselling, referral and linkage to schemes, rehabilitation, advocacy, research.
questions.question: What is a social problem? Discuss poverty and substance abuse as social problems, with their effects on health and the role of the nurse.

questions.answer:
1. Vulnerable group: at higher risk of poverty, exclusion, ill health and exploitation, with less power to protect itself.
2. Elderly: chronic disease, loneliness, neglect – Senior Citizens Act 2007, old-age pensions, Atal Vayo Abhyuday Yojana.
3. Persons with disabilities: stigma, inaccessibility, unemployment – RPWD Act 2016.
4. Minorities: discrimination – Articles 29–30.
5. SC and ST, women, children, transgender persons (Transgender Persons Act 2019, SMILE), migrants, homeless, people with mental illness or HIV.
6. Fundamental rights: equality (14–18), freedom (19–22, with 21 life and 21A education), against exploitation (23–24), religion (25–28), cultural and educational (29–30), constitutional remedies (32).
7. Women: Articles 14, 15, 15(3), 16, 23; Article 42 maternity relief; laws on dowry, domestic violence, child marriage, sex selection.
8. Children: Articles 21A, 24, 15(3), 45; Article 51A(k) duty of parents; UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.
9. Nurse: identify, educate about rights and schemes, counsel, refer, advocate, rehabilitate, report as law requires.
questions.question: Describe the vulnerable groups in society. Explain the fundamental rights of individuals, women and children, and the role of the nurse.

questions.answer:
1. Work that deprives children of childhood, schooling and health.
2. Causes: poverty, large families, illiterate parents, demand for cheap labour, debt.
3. Health effects: injuries, chemicals and dust, malnutrition, stunting, abuse, no education.
4. Law: Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986 bans children in all occupations (limited exceptions) and adolescents in hazardous work; Article 24; RTE Act 2009.
5. Measures: rescue and rehabilitation, school enrolment and meals, family income support.
6. Nurse: identify, educate parents, refer to child protection services.
questions.question: Write a short note on child labour.

questions.answer:
1. An offence or anti-social act by a child below 18 years; called a 'child in conflict with law' under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act 2015.
2. Causes: broken or poor families, neglect, bad company, school failure, poverty, substance use, media, lack of recreation.
3. Dealt with by Juvenile Justice Boards; aim is reform, not punishment.
4. Measures: family support, school counselling, recreation, observation and special homes with education and training, after-care.
5. Nurse: identify at-risk children, counsel families, refer, promote healthy recreation.
questions.question: Write a short note on juvenile delinquency.

questions.answer:
1. Dowry: money, property or goods given or demanded in connection with marriage.
2. Causes: tradition, status display, son preference, greed, social pressure.
3. Effects: debt, harassment, domestic violence, suicide, dowry deaths, female foeticide, neglect of girls.

1. Crisis (Caplan): acute emotional upset when usual coping fails in the face of a stressful event; time-limited, usually four to six weeks.
2. Types: maturational (adolescence, marriage, retirement); situational (illness, death, job loss); adventitious (floods, riots, epidemics).

# Unit 1: Introduction to sociology, basic social concepts and social groups

This notes file covers INC Unit I (Introduction, 1 hour) and the first part of INC Unit II (Social structure): society, community, association, institution, the individual and society, personal disorganization and social groups. The rest of Unit II is in notes file 2.

## 1.1 What sociology is

The word **sociology** comes from the Latin *socius* (companion, associate) and the Greek *logos* (study or science). So, word for word, it is "the study of companionship", that is, of people living together.

The term was first used by the French thinker **Auguste Comte** (1798–1857), who is called the **father of sociology**. He wanted a science of society that studied social life by observation, the way natural sciences study nature.

**Definitions** (learn one or two and write them with the name):

| Writer | Definition in short |
| --- | --- |
| Auguste Comte | The science of social phenomena, studied by observation and classification |
| Max Weber | The science that tries to understand social action and so explain its course and effects |
| Émile Durkheim | The science of social institutions and social facts |
| MacIver and Page | Sociology is about social relationships; the network of relationships is called society |
| Ginsberg | The study of human interactions and inter-relations, their conditions and consequences |

A simple working definition for the exam: **sociology is the scientific study of human society, social relationships, social groups and social institutions, and of how they change.**

## 1.2 Nature of sociology

1. **An independent social science** – it has its own subject matter (social relationships) and is not a branch of philosophy or history.
2. **A social science, not a physical science** – it studies people and their relations, not matter.
3. **A categorical (positive) science, not a normative one** – it describes what *is*, not what *ought to be*; it does not pass moral judgement.
4. **A pure science, not an applied one** – its main aim is knowledge; but its findings are applied in nursing, medicine, social work, law and planning.
5. **An abstract science** – it studies patterns (family, caste, marriage), not one particular family or event.
6. **A generalizing science** – it looks for general rules that hold across many societies.
7. **Both rational and empirical** – it uses reasoning and also facts collected by observation, surveys and case studies.

## 1.3 Scope of sociology

There are two classic views of the scope.

**1. Formal (specialistic) school** – Georg Simmel, Max Weber, Tönnies, Vierkandt. Sociology should study only the *forms* of social relationships (cooperation, competition, conflict, domination, subordination), not their content, so that it stays a separate, specialised science.

**2. Synthetic school** – Émile Durkheim, L. T. Hobhouse, Sorokin, Ginsberg. Society is a whole; all parts are related, so sociology should be a general science that brings together the findings of all social sciences.

Most textbooks combine the two. In practical terms the scope covers:

- social structure – groups, communities, associations, institutions
- social processes – cooperation, competition, conflict, accommodation, assimilation
- social institutions – family, marriage, religion, education, economy, government
- social stratification – caste, class, race, social mobility
- culture and socialization
- social control and social change
- social problems and social disorganization
- special fields: medical sociology (sociology of health and illness), rural and urban sociology, sociology of the family, criminology, clinical sociology

## 1.4 Significance of sociology in nursing

Illness is never only a biological event; it happens to a person who lives in a family, a caste, a religion, a village or a slum. Sociology helps the nurse see that person.

| How sociology helps | Example in nursing |
| --- | --- |
| Understanding the patient as a social being | A daily-wage worker may leave hospital early because the family has no other earner |
| Understanding family and its role in care | Joint families often take decisions together; the nurse involves the right family member |
| Respecting culture, beliefs and customs | Food taboos after delivery, fasting, preference for a female nurse |
| Understanding social causes of disease | Poverty, overcrowding, illiteracy, unsafe water, addiction |
| Community health nursing | Knowing village structure, leaders, caste groups and local health practices helps in planning programmes |
| Health education | Messages are shaped to the group's language, values and literacy |
| Working in the hospital as a social system | Nurses understand roles, status, hierarchy and teamwork |
| Identifying vulnerable groups | Elderly, disabled, women, children, migrants, tribal people |
| Rehabilitation | Helping a patient return to family, work and community after illness or disability |
| Professional adjustment | Nursing itself is a social role with expectations, ethics and status |
| Social change | Nurses adapt to new technology, urbanization and changing family forms |

Remember the one-line idea: **sociology helps the nurse give holistic, culturally appropriate, family- and community-centred care.**

## 1.5 Society

**Society** is a web (network) of social relationships. MacIver and Page called it "a web of social relationships" that keeps changing. People living together over time, with a common culture and a sense of belonging, form a society.

**Characteristics of society**

1. **Likeness** – members share some common features (language, needs, culture).
2. **Difference** – there is also variety (age, sex, occupation); differences make division of labour possible.
3. **Interdependence** – no member is self-sufficient; the farmer, doctor, nurse and teacher need each other.
4. **Cooperation and conflict** – both exist; cooperation holds society together, controlled conflict brings change.
5. **Society is abstract** – relationships cannot be seen; only people and their behaviour can.
6. **Society is dynamic** – it changes all the time.
7. **Society has culture** – each society has its own way of life.
8. **Society is wider than any group** – it includes many groups, communities and institutions.

## 1.6 Community

A **community** is a group of people living in a **definite locality** who share a **common life** and have a **sense of belonging** ("we-feeling"). A village, a town, a tribal hamlet and a housing colony are communities.

Characteristics:

- a definite **locality** (territory)
- **community sentiment** – we-feeling, role feeling and dependency feeling
- common life, common customs, often a common language or dialect
- it is **natural** – people are born into it; it is not created for a purpose
- it is **permanent** and has its own name
- it is **wider** than an association; it meets most of a person's needs

## 1.7 Association

An **association** is a group **deliberately organised** to pursue one or more **specific common interests**. Examples: Trained Nurses' Association of India, a trade union, a cricket club, a political party, a women's self-help group.

Characteristics:

- formed for a definite purpose
- has rules, a constitution and office bearers
- membership is voluntary (in most cases)
- it is temporary – it may end when its aim is met
- it is a concrete group of people

## 1.8 Institution

An **institution** is an established, approved **way (procedure) of doing things** in a society. It is a system of rules and norms, not a group of people. Marriage, family, religion, education, property and government are institutions.

Characteristics: built around a basic social need; relatively permanent; has rules and procedures; has symbols (wedding ring, flag, uniform); passed from one generation to the next; abstract.

### Difference between community, association and institution

| Point | Community | Association | Institution |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Meaning | People in a locality with a common life | People organised for a specific purpose | Established procedure or set of rules |
| Nature | Concrete | Concrete | Abstract |
| Origin | Grows naturally | Deliberately formed | Grows slowly through custom and law |
| Membership | By birth or residence | Voluntary | One does not "join" it; one follows it |
| Duration | Permanent | Can be temporary | Long lasting |
| Example | A village | Trained Nurses' Association of India | Marriage |

A useful link: **a hospital is an association; the system of hospital care and its rules is an institution; the town in which it stands is a community.**

## 1.9 Individual and society

The relationship between the individual and society is two-way.

**Theories**

- **Social contract theory** (Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau): people originally lived in a "state of nature" and made an agreement (contract) to form society for protection. It is criticised because no such historical contract is known.
- **Organic theory** (Herbert Spencer): society is like a living body; individuals are its cells and institutions its organs. It shows interdependence but ignores that individuals have free will.
- **Group mind theory**: society has a mind of its own beyond individual minds; it is largely rejected.
- **Modern view**: the individual and society **make each other**. Society shapes the individual through socialization, and individuals shape society through their actions.

**Evidence that a person becomes "human" only in society** – reported cases of children reared in isolation (such as the girls known as Kamala and Amala found in Bengal, and the American child Anna) showed that without social contact a child does not learn language, emotional bonds or ordinary human behaviour.

**What society gives the individual**: protection, food and shelter through cooperation, language, culture, education, identity, status and role.

**What the individual gives society**: work, new ideas, leadership, and the transmission of culture to the next generation.

## 1.10 Personal disorganization

**Personal disorganization** is a state in which an individual's behaviour **deviates from the accepted norms** of the group so that he or she cannot fulfil social roles, and personal life and relationships break down. Elliott and Merrill describe it as the opposite of personal organization.

**Forms (examples)**: alcoholism and drug addiction, crime and delinquency, suicide and attempted suicide, prostitution, mental illness, vagrancy and beggary, gambling.

**Causes**

| Group | Causes |
| --- | --- |
| Personal | Physical or mental illness, disability, frustration, low self-esteem |
| Family | Broken home, death or desertion of a parent, domestic violence, neglect |
| Economic | Poverty, unemployment, debt |
| Social | Rapid social change, migration, loss of traditional controls, bad company |
| Cultural | Conflict between old and new values, culture shock |

**Role of the nurse**: identify early signs (withdrawal, absence from work, injuries, substance use), listen without judging, refer to counsellor, de-addiction centre or social worker, involve the family, and teach healthy coping.

## 1.11 Social groups

A **social group** is two or more people who **interact** with one another, share a **sense of unity** and have **common interests or goals**. A crowd waiting at a bus stop is an aggregate, not a group, because there is no interaction or we-feeling.

**Characteristics of a social group**

1. Two or more members
2. Reciprocal relationships and interaction
3. Sense of unity ("we-feeling")
4. Common interest or goal
5. Group norms that regulate behaviour
6. A structure – roles, statuses, often a leader
7. Groups are dynamic; they change over time

**Classification of social groups**

| Basis | Types | Given by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Closeness of contact | **Primary** and **secondary** groups | C. H. Cooley (primary); secondary added later |
| Sense of belonging | **In-group** ("we") and **out-group** ("they") | W. G. Sumner |
| Way of formation | **Voluntary** and **involuntary** groups | – |
| Size | Small and large groups | Simmel |
| Organisation | Formal and informal groups | – |
| Life of the group | Temporary and permanent | – |
| Point of reference | **Reference group** – a group whose standards a person uses to judge himself | Herbert Hyman, R. K. Merton |
| Type of bond | **Gemeinschaft** (community, close ties) and **Gesellschaft** (association, impersonal ties) | Ferdinand Tönnies |

### Primary and secondary groups

| Feature | Primary group | Secondary group |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Example | Family, play group, close neighbours | Hospital, university, trade union, political party |
| Size | Small | Large |
| Contact | Face to face, intimate | Indirect, formal |
| Relationship | Personal, for its own sake | Impersonal, for a purpose |
| Duration | Long lasting | May be temporary |
| Control | Informal (praise, blame) | Formal (rules, law) |
| Role in life | Shapes personality; "nursery of human nature" (Cooley) | Meets special needs |

### Importance of groups in nursing

- The family (primary group) is the first caregiver and decision maker.
- Patients in a ward form small groups; group health teaching and support groups (diabetes, cancer, de-addiction) use group strength.
- The nursing team is a formal group; good teamwork depends on clear roles and communication.
- Reference groups influence health behaviour – adolescents copy peers in smoking or dieting.

## Remember

- Sociology = scientific study of society and social relationships; **Auguste Comte** is the father of sociology and coined the term.
- Nature: independent, social, categorical, pure, abstract, generalizing, rational and empirical science.
- Scope: formal school (Simmel, Weber) vs synthetic school (Durkheim, Hobhouse).
- Society = web of social relationships; community = locality + we-feeling; association = organised for a purpose; institution = established procedure.
- Personal disorganization = an individual's failure to follow norms and fulfil roles.
- Primary group (Cooley): small, face to face, intimate – the family is the best example.
- In-group/out-group (Sumner); Gemeinschaft/Gesellschaft (Tönnies); reference group (Hyman, Merton).

# Unit 2: Social processes, socialization, social change and communities

This notes file covers the second part of INC Unit II (Social structure, 15 hours in all): social processes, socialization, social change and the role of the nurse, urban, rural and tribal communities with their health problems, and the importance of social structure in nursing.

## 2.1 Social processes

**Social interaction** is the mutual action and reaction between people or groups. When interaction takes a repeated, recognisable form, it is called a **social process**. Ginsberg describes social processes as the various modes of interaction between individuals or groups, including cooperation, conflict, differentiation and integration.

Social processes are of two broad kinds:

```text
                   Social processes
                         |
        +----------------+----------------+
        |                                 |
  Associative (conjunctive)        Dissociative (disjunctive)
  bring people together            push people apart
  - cooperation                    - competition
  - accommodation                  - conflict
  - assimilation                   - (isolation, the absence
                                      of interaction)
```

### Cooperation

**Cooperation** is working together for a common goal. It is the most basic process; family, society and every health team depend on it.

- **Direct cooperation** – people do the same work together (villagers building a well).
- **Indirect cooperation** – people do different but related work for a common end (division of labour in a hospital: doctor, nurse, pharmacist, laboratory technician).
- **Primary** (in primary groups), **secondary** (in organisations) and **tertiary** (temporary cooperation between groups with different aims, such as two political parties joining for an election) – classification by Ogburn and Nimkoff.

Nursing example: the nurse, patient and family cooperate in a home care plan.

### Competition

**Competition** is a struggle between people for things that are limited (jobs, seats, prizes, status), usually **impersonal, continuous, unconscious** of the rival and **governed by rules**.

- Effects: it can raise efficiency and progress, but too much competition causes anxiety, frustration and conflict.
- Example: competition for admission to nursing colleges.

### Conflict

**Conflict** is a struggle in which people or groups try to achieve their ends by **opposing or harming the rival**, directly and consciously.

- Characteristics: personal and conscious, intermittent (not continuous), may involve threat or violence.
- Types (Gillin and Gillin): personal, racial, class, political and international conflict.
- Effects: harmful when violent, but controlled conflict can lead to change and greater unity within each group.
- Example: a quarrel between the patient's relatives and hospital staff; land disputes in a village.

### Accommodation

**Accommodation** is the process of **adjusting to a conflict** so that people with differences can live and work together, without the differences disappearing.

Methods: coercion (force), compromise, arbitration and conciliation, toleration, conversion, sublimation (redirecting energy into acceptable work), rationalization.

Example: a new nurse adjusts to the routines of a ward; two quarrelling departments agree to a shared roster.

### Assimilation

**Assimilation** is a slow, **unconscious** process by which individuals or groups with different cultures **merge** and take on a common culture, so that the original differences fade.

- Factors that help: tolerance, long contact, intermarriage, common economic life, education, cultural similarity.
- Factors that hinder: isolation, prejudice, very different cultures, physical differences, feelings of superiority.
- Example: migrant families in a city slowly adopt city language, dress and food.

**Accommodation vs assimilation**: accommodation is quicker and conscious, and differences remain; assimilation is slow and unconscious, and differences disappear.

### Isolation

**Isolation** is the absence of social contact or communication. It may be physical (geographical remoteness, hospital isolation ward), social (untouchability, stigma of leprosy, HIV or mental illness) or psychological (loneliness of the elderly). Prolonged isolation harms personality and mental health. The nurse reduces isolation by communication, involving family and support groups, and fighting stigma.

## 2.2 Socialization

**Socialization** is the lifelong process by which an individual **learns the culture, norms, values and roles** of the society and becomes a functioning member of it. It turns a biological infant into a social being.

### Characteristics

1. It is **lifelong** – from birth to death (childhood, school, marriage, work, old age).
2. It **transmits culture** from one generation to the next.
3. It is learned through **interaction**.
4. It **varies** between societies and over time.
5. It creates **self and personality**.
6. It can be **conscious** (teaching) or **unconscious** (imitation).

### Process (stages)

Two widely taught explanations:

**Charles Horton Cooley – the "looking-glass self"**: a person develops a self-image by imagining (1) how he appears to others, (2) how others judge that appearance, and (3) feeling pride or shame as a result.

**George Herbert Mead – development of self**:

```text
I (spontaneous self) ⇌ Me (social self, the attitudes of others taken in)

Stage 1 Imitation (preparatory) – the child copies actions without understanding
Stage 2 Play stage – the child plays one role at a time ("mother", "doctor")
Stage 3 Game stage – the child understands many roles at once and the rules
        (the "generalized other": the expectations of society as a whole)
```

**Sigmund Freud** – personality grows through the id, ego and superego; the superego (conscience) is formed by taking in the parents' and society's rules.

Stages across life (common textbook form): primary socialization in infancy and childhood, secondary socialization in school and peer groups, adult socialization (marriage, work, parenthood), **anticipatory socialization** (learning a role before taking it, e.g. a student nurse learning professional behaviour) and **resocialization** (learning new ways after a major change – retirement, disability, prison, migration).

### Agencies of socialization

| Agency | What it teaches |
| --- | --- |
| **Family** – the first and most important agency | Language, habits, hygiene, values, gender roles, love and trust |
| Peer group (play group) | Cooperation, competition, equality, social skills |
| School and teachers | Knowledge, discipline, citizenship, punctuality |
| Religion | Morals, rituals, beliefs about life, illness and death |
| Neighbourhood and community | Customs, festivals, local norms |
| Mass media and the internet | Ideas, fashion, attitudes – both good and harmful (advertising of junk food, tobacco) |
| Occupation and workplace | Professional roles, ethics (nursing code of conduct) |
| State and law | Rights, duties, discipline |

### Nurse and socialization

- Professional socialization turns a student into a nurse – learning skills, ethics, uniform, accountability.
- A patient admitted to hospital goes through **resocialization** – learning the "sick role", ward routines, a new diet or insulin.
- The nurse teaches families healthy habits and so becomes an agent of socialization for health.

## 2.3 Social change

**Social change** is a **change in the social structure and social relationships** of a society over time – in its institutions, roles, values and way of life. (MacIver and Page: changes in social relationships.)

### Nature (characteristics)

- It is **universal** – every society changes.
- It is **continuous** but its **speed varies** between societies and periods.
- It is **community change**, not change in one person.
- It is **unpredictable** in detail.
- It can be **planned** (family planning, literacy campaigns) or **unplanned** (natural disaster, epidemic).
- It may be **progress** or **regress**; change itself is value-neutral.

### Factors (causes) of social change

| Factor | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Demographic | Population growth, falling death rate, ageing, migration |
| Technological | Vaccines, mobile phones, telemedicine, mechanised farming |
| Economic | Industrialization, new jobs, income changes |
| Cultural | New ideas, education, values |
| Political and legal | New laws on marriage, dowry, child labour |
| Biological and natural | Epidemics such as COVID-19, floods, droughts |
| Education and communication | Literacy, media, internet |

### Process of social change

Change usually spreads through **invention** (a new idea or tool), **discovery**, **diffusion** (spread from one group to another) and **acculturation** (one culture taking traits from another). Common processes in India are **Sanskritization** (a lower caste adopting customs of higher castes to raise its status – M. N. Srinivas), **Westernization**, **modernization**, **urbanization** and **industrialization**.

**Cultural lag** (W. F. Ogburn): material culture (technology) changes faster than non-material culture (beliefs, customs), creating a gap – for example, hospital delivery is available but some families still prefer untrained home delivery.

### Theories in brief

- **Linear (evolutionary)** – society moves forward in stages (Comte, Spencer).
- **Cyclical** – societies rise and fall in cycles (Spengler, Toynbee, Sorokin).
- **Conflict** – change comes from class struggle (Karl Marx).
- **Functional** – change is a slow adjustment that keeps balance (Talcott Parsons).

### Role of the nurse in social change

1. **Change agent** – introduces healthy practices (hand washing, breastfeeding, immunization).
2. **Health educator** – removes harmful beliefs gently while respecting culture.
3. **Researcher** – finds out which practices help or harm.
4. **Adapting to change** – learns new technology, digital records, new disease patterns.
5. **Advocate** – supports laws and programmes for women, children and the elderly.
6. **Counsellor** – helps families cope with change (migration, nuclear family stress, ageing parents living alone).
7. **Leader** – plans change step by step: understand the community, involve leaders, start small, evaluate.

## 2.4 Urban, rural and tribal communities

### Rural community

Characteristics: small population living in villages; agriculture and allied work as the main occupation; close relation with nature; primary relationships (everyone knows everyone); joint families more common; strong caste, religion and tradition; panchayat and elders exercise control; simple living; slower social change; lower literacy and fewer services.

### Urban community

Characteristics: large, dense, mixed population; non-agricultural occupations (industry, trade, services); division of labour and specialisation; secondary, impersonal relationships; nuclear families more common; social mobility and individualism; formal control (police, law); faster change; better access to schools and hospitals, but also slums and pollution.

### Rural vs urban

| Point | Rural | Urban |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Size and density | Small, scattered | Large, dense |
| Occupation | Agriculture | Industry, trade, services |
| Relationships | Primary, personal | Secondary, impersonal |
| Family | Joint more common | Nuclear more common |
| Control | Informal – customs, elders | Formal – law, police |
| Mobility | Low | High |
| Change | Slow | Fast |
| Services | Fewer | More, but unequal |

### Tribal community

Tribes (Scheduled Tribes in the Constitution) are communities that usually live in forests, hills or remote areas. Characteristics: a common territory and a common name; their own dialect; strong kinship and clan ties; endogamy within the tribe; simple economy (hunting, gathering, shifting cultivation, forest produce); own customs, beliefs and traditional healers; a tribal council or chief for control; relative isolation from the mainstream.

### Major health problems

| Community | Major health problems |
| --- | --- |
| Rural | Communicable diseases (diarrhoea, typhoid, tuberculosis), malnutrition and anaemia, maternal and child health problems, unsafe water and open defecation, snake bite and farm injuries, pesticide poisoning, delayed care because of distance, reliance on untrained practitioners |
| Urban | Lifestyle diseases (diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, cancer), obesity, air and noise pollution, road traffic accidents, stress and mental illness, substance abuse, slum problems (overcrowding, tuberculosis, vector-borne disease), HIV and STIs, occupational diseases |
| Tribal | Malaria and other vector-borne disease, malnutrition, anaemia, genetic disorders such as sickle cell disease in some groups, high maternal and infant illness, skin and worm infections, alcohol use, poor access to services, mistrust of outsiders |

## 2.5 Importance of social structure in nursing

**Social structure** is the relatively stable pattern of social relationships, roles, statuses, groups and institutions in a society. Knowing it helps the nurse to:

- plan care that fits the family, caste, religion and community of the patient
- identify leaders and decision makers for community programmes
- understand why some groups use services less (distance, cost, caste barriers, gender norms)
- find vulnerable groups and target help to them
- work within the hospital's own structure of roles and authority
- use local institutions – panchayats, self-help groups, schools, ASHAs and anganwadis – to spread health messages

## Remember

- Associative processes: cooperation, accommodation, assimilation. Dissociative: competition, conflict.
- Competition = impersonal, continuous; conflict = personal, conscious, intermittent.
- Accommodation adjusts to conflict (differences stay); assimilation merges cultures (differences fade).
- Socialization = lifelong learning of culture; family is the first and most important agency.
- Cooley – looking-glass self; Mead – I and me, play and game stages, generalized other.
- Social change is universal and continuous; cultural lag (Ogburn); Sanskritization (M. N. Srinivas).
- Nurse = change agent, health educator, advocate, counsellor.
- Rural – agriculture, primary ties, communicable disease; urban – industry, impersonal ties, lifestyle disease; tribal – isolation, malaria, malnutrition, sickle cell in some groups.
